title: How C# code becomes running programs (source, IL, JIT, AOT)
hook: A C# file is not executed as plain text. The Roslyn compiler turns it into Intermediate Language (IL) inside an assembly, and the Common Language Runtime (CLR) compiles that to machine code when your app runs — or ahead of time if you choose Native Ahead-of-Time (AOT).

blocks.text: The compilation pipeline is the journey from your .cs source files to code the CPU can execute. Roslyn (the C# compiler) reads your code and emits IL plus rich metadata packaged as an assembly (.dll or .exe). At run time, the CLR's Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler turns each method's IL into native machine instructions. Native AOT is an alternative: it compiles to a standalone native binary before deployment, trading some flexibility for faster startup.

entries.plainDefinition: The official open-source compiler that turns C# source into IL assemblies.
entries.example: dotnet build invokes Roslyn behind the scenes.

entries.plainDefinition: The part of the CLR that compiles IL to machine code at run time, method by method.
entries.example: The first call to a method triggers JIT compilation; later calls reuse the native code.

entries.plainDefinition: Compiling to native machine code before the app runs, instead of waiting for JIT at startup.
entries.example: Setting PublishAot=true produces a native binary with no JIT step at launch.

blocks.text: Understanding the pipeline explains build output, deployment size, cold-start behavior, and why C# is not "interpreted like a script." When two microservices share a domain model, they reference the same assembly — a versioned, metadata-rich unit. JavaScript modules are a file graph resolved by the host; a .NET assembly can hold many types, resources, and version information. Binding failures look like FileNotFoundException, not ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND.

blocks.title: When interviewers ask "is C# compiled or interpreted?"
blocks.body: Say compiled twice: Roslyn compiles to IL at build time, and the JIT (or AOT) compiles IL to CPU code. It is never a line-by-line interpreter like an old BASIC shell.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Write .cs files
items.body: Your C# source lives in the project. Folders are organizational; the compiler reads all included files.

items.title: Roslyn emits IL + metadata
items.body: The compiler produces an assembly (.dll) containing IL instructions and type metadata the CLR needs.

items.title: CLR loads the assembly
items.body: At startup, the runtime verifies types, resolves references, and prepares methods.

items.title: JIT or AOT produces machine code
items.body: Default path: JIT compiles methods on demand with tiered optimization. AOT path: everything is native before launch.

diagram.title: Compilation pipeline
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  A[C# source .cs] --> B[Roslyn compiler]
  B --> C[IL + metadata in assembly]
  C --> D{Run mode}
  D -->|Default| E[CLR JIT]
  D -->|PublishAot| F[Native AOT binary]
  E --> G[CPU machine code]
  F --> G

snippet.label: Simple worker source
snippet.explanation: Even a one-liner becomes IL in an assembly. There is no direct "run the .cs text" path in a normal SDK project — the compiler always sits in between.

snippet.label: Enable Native AOT publish
snippet.code:
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <PublishAot>true</PublishAot>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>

<!-- dotnet publish -c Release produces a native binary -->
snippet.explanation: AOT compiles ahead of deployment. Useful for cold-start-sensitive workloads (like short-lived Lambdas), but reflection-heavy libraries may need PublishAot=false.

snippet.label: Inspect build output
snippet.code:
dotnet build -c Release
ls bin/Release/net10.0/
# Worker.dll  — IL assembly
# Worker.deps.json — dependency manifest
# Worker.runtimeconfig.json — runtime settings
snippet.explanation: dotnet build produces IL assemblies and manifests — not JavaScript. Compare this to tsc emitting .js files with no CLR metadata.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Saying C# is "interpreted" — it is compiled; JIT is a second compile, not line-by-line interpretation. Confusing C# language version (LangVersion) with Target Framework Moniker (TFM) — LangVersion controls syntax; net10.0 controls which runtime APIs exist. Assuming Native AOT is always on — SDK projects default to JIT unless you enable PublishAot.

interviewTakeaways: C# compile output is IL + metadata in an assembly; JIT or Native AOT produces CPU code.
Do not equate `import "./worker.js"` with referencing a .NET assembly.
AOT trades flexibility (reflection, runtime codegen) for startup and size — know when a consumer needs JIT instead.
commonPitfalls: Saying C# is "interpreted." It is compiled; the JIT is a second compile, not a line-by-line interpreter.
Confusing the C# language version with the TFM. LangVersion is syntax; net10.0 is the runtime surface.
Assuming Native AOT is always on. SDK projects default to JIT unless you enable PublishAot (file-based apps enable it for publish).

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript modules are source or bytecode files the engine links at load time. .NET assemblies are IL plus metadata units versioned and loaded by the CLR.
